summary: Greece is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorization being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90, applied for through Greek consulates and visa centers.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.
For stays over 90 days: work, family reunification and other long-stay purposes. Confirm the fee for your category with the Greek consulate, as some categories differ.
Required for courses longer than 90 days; needs proof of enrollment, funds and health insurance. Confirm the current fee with the Greek consulate.

For remote workers employed by or contracting with non-Greek companies; income requirement of at least €3,500 net per month (plus 20% for a spouse, 15% per child). Confirm current figures with the consulate.
Requires prior approval of the employment position in Greece before the visa application; converted to a residence permit after arrival.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Greece expects non-EU visitors to show roughly €50 per person per day, with a minimum total of around €300 for stays up to 5 days. Confirm current figures with the Greek consulate.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards are widely accepted in cities and tourist areas, but small tavernas, kiosks and businesses on smaller islands often prefer cash. Carry euros, especially outside the main resorts.

safety.text: Greece is a very safe destination with low violent crime. Watch for pickpocketing on the Athens metro and in crowded tourist areas, and follow local guidance during summer wildfire alerts.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Greece Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–June and September–October offer warm seas and open island infrastructure without the July–August heat, crowds and peak ferry prices; Athens and the mainland are pleasant even in early spring and late fall.

idp.text: Greece is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Greece is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Greece yet.

tips.text: Tap water is safe in Athens, Thessaloniki and most of the mainland, but on many islands (including Santorini and much of the Cyclades) it is desalinated or brackish. Drink bottled water there.
Island ferries are weather-dependent and can be canceled at short notice in high winds — don't book a ferry arriving the same day as your flight home, and reserve popular summer routes in advance.
Smaller islands have few ATMs and they can run dry in peak season — withdraw cash before leaving Athens or the main port towns, and avoid dynamic currency conversion at tourist-area ATMs.
Apply for ETIAS only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site once it becomes mandatory — unofficial sites charge inflated fees.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Greece?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Greece and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Greece Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries, including island hopping anywhere in Greece.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Greece?
faq.answer: ETIAS is being phased in for visa-exempt travelers. During the transition period travelers without ETIAS are still admitted; once fully mandatory, the €20 online authorization will be required before boarding. Check the official EU website for the current status.

faq.question: Does Greece have a digital nomad visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Greece's digital nomad visa (around €75) is for remote workers employed by non-Greek companies with a net income of at least €3,500 per month. It is issued for up to a year and can be converted into a two-year digital nomad residence permit in Greece.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Greece without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area — time in Greece and other Schengen countries shares the same allowance. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but must register locally after 3 months.
